articles.title: Anthony Davis Trade Idea Could Be Golden State Warriors' Last Hope
articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors are, in a lot of ways, living on borrowed time.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors are, in a lot of ways, living on borrowed time.

Steve Kerr nearly called it quits this offseason. Draymond Green sounded halfway out the door at last season's trade deadline. Stephen Curry was confronting his "basketball mortality" after a recent injury—the runner's knee that cost him two months last season, not the oblique abdominal tear derailing this one.

They could have waived the white flag by now. Some will argue they should have.

Yet, somewhere in the deep recesses of their minds, there's still enough what-if hope that some basketball magic remains in front of them. What if Curry and Jimmy Butler are healthy when it matters most? What if they're already developing a third star in breakout rookie Yaxel Lendeborg?

What if the trade market happens to bear the kind of high-end talent needed to both withstand this current Curry-less, Butler-less stretch and to enjoy meaningful success upon their return? Because there might be a way to add an established elite without giving up Butler or gutting their collection of draft capital.

It all revolves around Anthony Davis, who held their attention this offseason and sounds very much ready for a scenery change now. Let's dig into all the hows and whys of finally bringing the Brow to the Bay.

Golden State Warriors receive: Anthony Davis

Washington Wizards receive: Draymond Green, Moses Moody, Kristaps Porziņģis, 2031 first-round pick swap (top-three protected), 2030 second-round pick, 2033 second-round pick

As long as Golden State's goal is to become, as Curry put it , "any semblance of a threat come the end of the year," then it has to find a long-term ceiling-raiser. And probably a short-term floor-raiser, too, since this Curry-less stretch has season-spoiling potential if things get really out of hand.

Davis checks both boxes better than anyone who is both available and relatively affordable (i.e., not a total drain on the draft capital). Now, that's obviously only true if he stays healthy, but he has been healthy so far. The injury risk tied to him is factored into the acquisition cost.

The Warriors have seemingly admitted the need for a major roster upgrade. They reportedly have the appetite for a significant trade. Davis clearly qualifies as such. Even if you remove his Hall of Fame-caliber credentials out of it, just look at what he's doing now: 24.6 points, 10.1 rebounds, 2.1 assists, 1.2 steals and 1.2 blocks.

He remains a legitimate difference-maker. His plus-8.6 net differential ranks in the 78th percentile across the Association.

The 33-year-old still moves the proverbial needle in ways that directly address the Dubs' needs: size, interior defense, rebounding, support scoring, and star power. He retains "demand" around the league, per ESPN's Brian Windhorst , though potential suitors "don't want to give him a max extension."

The Warriors surely share that hesitation. If they make a trade-season splash, they'll probably look for someone who either won't cut into their post-Curry flexibility or fits Lendeborg's timeline. Davis could qualify for the former. For all the talk about a new deal, his $62.8 million player option for next season might be too tempting to pass up.

If Golden State could convince Davis to lock in for this season and next—or maybe agree to an arrangement that extends slightly beyond that—it could still have hope.

The Warriors aren't one trade away from joining the NBA's elite tier, but they could be lucky on the health front, short of putting a true scare into the teams that are. Tag a big, ole *if healthy* asterisk onto this, but a Curry-Butler-Lendeborg-Davis foursome would be legitimately ferocious come playoff time.

When Davis and the Wizards tabled extension talks before the season, it seemed both sides wanted more time to get to know each other. Those verdicts must be rendered by now, right?

While Davis still looks like a winning player, Washington obviously isn't ready to win with him. The Trae Young extension appears to be a major misfire. AJ Dybantsa is going through the growing pains encountered by most rookies. The young core is still taking shape around him.

Whatever elevation the Wizards thought was possible this season isn't happening. This is a bottom-third team by effectively all metrics, and any hope for a notable turnaround would stem from little more than glass-overflowing optimism.

Washington should get real about its situation. It brokered discounted deals for Davis and Young last season to see what impact those veterans might have on this young roster. It already has the answer.

The Wizards prematurely locked Young into their long-term plans. They should not make the same mistake with Davis.

Now, is this an overwhelming amount of assets? Not at all, but a Davis deal isn't providing that. Not with his contract uncertainty looming overhead.

This would, however, deliver immediate financial relief—Green is on an expiring contract, and Porziņģis effectively is ($3 million guaranteed for next season)—and some helpful pieces for the future. Green could offer some present-day value, too, either attracting interest on the trade market or at least imparting all kinds of defensive smarts into this young core.

Moody, 24, sits somewhere between a rotation-regular and a solid starter. The Wizards have some intriguing, young wings, but no NBA team can ever be too deep in that department. The pick swap could hold immense value since it would almost certainly come after the Warriors' Curry chapter has closed. The same might hold true for both incoming second-round picks.

As much as Washington wants to accelerate this rebuilding process, it can't ignore the obvious signs of this roster's lack of readiness. Turning Davis into flexibility and future assets would better align the organization around its new crown jewel in Dybantsa.

articles.title: Ranking The Rock's 10 Greatest WWE Moments Ahead of 30th Anniversary at Survivor Series
articles.summary: The Rock's return at Survivor Series 2026 will mark 30 years since his televised WWE in-ring debut at the event.
articles.body:
The Rock's return at Survivor Series 2026 will mark 30 years since his televised WWE in-ring debut at the event.

It's unknown what he'll have in store for his appearance, but WWE has spent this month highlighting his most memorable milestones—of which there are many—to commemorate the occasion.

Rock rapidly ascended the ranks in WWE and was a world champion within two years of his arrival. He excelled as both a babyface and a heel, took part in countless classic matches and captured a slew of championships before taking his talents to Hollywood.

Although he hasn't been full-time with the company since the early 2000s, he's had several return runs where he's routinely reminded fans just why he's among the best of all-time. It isn't uncommon for him to be included in the Mt. Rushmore conversation, not only because he was virtually the complete package as a performer but also for his long list of achievements and transcending the industry.

Ahead of his upcoming anniversary at Survivor Series, these are the top 10 greatest moments of his illustrious career, ranked.

10. A Rocky Arrival (Survivor Series 1996)

The Rock made his televised in-ring debut for WWE at Survivor Series 1996 as Rocky Maivia, combining the monikers of his father, Rocky Johnson, and his grandfather "High Chief" Peter Maivia.

It was as part of a classic Survivor Series elimination tag team match, teaming with Jake Roberts, Marc Mero and Barry Windham (then known as The Stalker) to take on Hunter Hearst Helmsley, Jerry Lawler, Crush and Goldust.

It was a perfect scenario for his introduction, as it allowed him to mix it up with top talent and benefit from beating them. Emerging as the sole survivor indicated big things were on the horizon for him, especially with that event emanating from the world-famous Madison Square Garden.

Of course, the blue-chipper Rocky Maivia character didn't stick, and it wasn't long before fans revolted against him. That later led into him joining The Nation of Domination and embracing the boos as a heel.

9. Ending a Decade-Long Drought (Royal Rumble 2013)

When The Rock originally returned to WWE in 2011, the endgame always appeared to be a WrestleMania match with John Cena. He was never expected to face anyone else or do much else beyond that because of how limited his appearance schedule was.

After shockingly winning that epic encounter with Cena, Rock turned his sights to a greater goal: becoming champion again. He hinted at challenging for the WWE Championship on the post-WrestleMania Raw in 2012, before finally making it official for the Royal Rumble on the 1,000th episode of Raw that summer.

WWE mastered the build for CM Punk vs. Rock at the Rumble. The two brought the best out of each other on the mic and made what was already a marquee match feel even bigger.

Punk had reigned as the WWE champ for a whopping 434 days going into the event, so it was a massive deal when Rock managed to be the one to end his run as well as his own decade-long drought without a world title.

That set the stage for a WrestleMania rematch between Rock and Cena that was inferior to the first.

8. The Final Boss Bloodies Cody Rhodes (Raw, March 25, 2024)

The Rock vs. Roman Reigns has been WWE's most fantasized dream match of the modern era. There were various points where the bout could have been booked, but Rock's sporadic schedule prevented those plans from coming to fruition.

The one year where it finally could have happened was the one year where it didn't make sense. Cody Rhodes had the fans firmly behind him as he looked to "finish his story" against Reigns at WrestleMania 40, only for Rock to resurface and attempt to steal that spot away from him.

Reigns vs. Rock was all but a lock for The Show of Shows until WWE pivoted back to Reigns vs. Rhodes and went in a wildly different direction with Rock going heel instead. It was a breath of fresh air for both Rock and the product itself, resulting in an exciting and unpredictable Road to WrestleMania.

The highlight of his heel run was his heinous attack on Rhodes on the March 25 edition of Raw, where he brutalized him outside of the arena and bloodied him in front of his own American Nightmare bus. Rock's repeated mentions of "Mama Rhodes" as he whipped him with his weight belt made for tremendous television.

We never quite did get a proper resolution to the Rock vs. Rhodes rivalry, but Rock's in-ring return in the tag team match on Night 1 of WrestleMania 40 was a successful one as he pinned Rhodes to clinch the victory.

Expectations for The Rock at Survivor Series ⭐

7. This Is Your Life (Raw, Sept. 27, 1999)

A number of The Rock's most memorable moments haven't necessarily been matches, championships or returns.

Sometimes it's been as simple as a segment or a promo, such as the hilarious rundown of all his opponents in the Armageddon Hell in a Cell match or the " Rock Concerts " he hosted while portraying Hollywood Rock.

Perhaps one of the most fun segments to come out of the Attitude Era was when Mankind held his own version of the 1950s television show This Is Your Life tailored to Rock's past by bringing back faces he was familiar with while trying to endear himself to his new tag team partner.

The guests included one of Rock's teachers from sixth grade, an old coach and his high school sweetheart. Each guest was worse than the last, and Rock no-selling the segment made Mankind's desperation for his affection even funnier.

More amazingly, these two were involved in a vicious "I Quit" match earlier in the year, and were now best buds (in Mankind's eyes, anyway).

This was a total train wreck in the best way possible, and served as the ultimate example of why The Brahma Bull is one of WWE's all-time entertainers with remarkable range.

WWE embarked on an unprecedented path by announcing The Rock vs. John Cena for WrestleMania 28 almost one year in advance, a night removed from Rock costing Cena the WWE Championship in the main event of WrestleMania 27.

It led to a lot of little reminders throughout that the match was made official for 'Mania the following year, with the hype not truly kicking into high gear until early 2012. At that point, they began interacting much more on television, trading verbal jabs and attempting to get the advantage over the other.

None of that mattered by WrestleMania, however. The atmosphere in Miami's Sun Life Stadium was electric, but if they couldn't deliver when the bell rang, it would have gone down as one of the biggest busts in WWE history, regardless of how much money that 'Mania generated from ticket sales and pay-per-view buys.

Sure enough, they had instant chemistry. It was less of a technical masterpiece than it was a thrilling clash between the top two titans in the industry, complete with arrogant showboating, suspenseful nearfalls and dramatic facial expressions.

Cena besting Rock so the torch could be passed (even though Cena had already solidified himself as a star years earlier) felt like a foregone conclusion, so Rock pulling out the W instead was a genuine (and satisfying) shocker for fans.

What was believed to be a one-off for Rock in the ring turned into a full-fledged return run and led to him winning the WWE Championship and headlining WrestleMania another two times over the next dozen years.

When The Rock returned to WWE with his heel Hollywood persona in early 2003, he made it clear that he had accomplished everything he had set out to do except for one thing: beating "Stone Cold" Steve Austin at WrestleMania.

The two waged war at WrestleMania in 1999 and 2001, and on both occasions, Austin had his hand raised in victory. Wanting to right that wrong, Rock challenged his career-long rival to one more match at WrestleMania 19, with the story essentially selling itself.

It was very much a "greatest hits" of their fantastic feud. The two traded finishers back and forth and managed to recreate that same magic they always had whenever they found themselves on opposite sides of the squared circle.

Fittingly, it took The Great One three Rock Bottoms to beat Austin and end their trilogy at WrestleMania in definitive fashion. It simultaneously marked the end of an era, with their days as full-time members of the roster forever behind them.

It was a wonderful swan song for the faces of the Attitude Era.

"Stone Cold" Steve Austin being sidelined for a majority of 2000 with a neck injury immediately made The Rock the de facto face of WWE, and as such, it was no surprise that he won the Royal Rumble match that year to punch his ticket to the main event of WrestleMania for the WWE Championship.

WWE took a slam dunk of a main event between Rock and reigning champ Triple H and muddied the waters by adding Big Show and recently-retired Mick Foley to make it an elimination four-way match. Worse yet, a McMahon was put in every corner so the focus was on the family and not the longstanding bad blood between Rock and HHH.

Triple H retaining the title was a disappointing outcome, but he and Rock ran it back one-on-one later that month at Backlash. There were still shenanigans (especially with Shane McMahon serving as the special guest referee) but not nearly as many, allowing them to have the top-tier main event they were capable of.

Just when it looked like the odds were stacked against Rock, Austin emerged to a legendary pop to level McMahon's goons and aid Rock to victory and the prestigious prize. It was the epitome of everything that made Attitude Era main events so exhilarating, and a return to form for Rock as WWE's biggest babyface.

3. A Long-Awaited Return (Raw, Feb. 14, 2011)

For years, John Cena trash-talked The Rock in interviews and criticized his choice to leave WWE to pursue an acting career in Hollywood.

It was fun to fantasy book a bout between the two, but Rock was so removed from the wrestling realm at the time that it seemed to be just that: a fantasy.

Although Rock inducted his father and grandfather into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2008 and made occasional taped appearances, he remained largely absent from WWE until 2011.

As WrestleMania 27 drew closer, rumors ran rampant regarding who the mystery host of the event would be and whether it could be the returning Rock. It felt like a likely possibility, but it was still surreal for the opening chords of his entrance music to hit the arena on the Valentine's Day edition of Raw in 2011.

Rock proceeded to not only declare himself the host of WrestleMania but also preach to the fans about being back "home" and take shots at everyone from Cena to then-WWE champion The Miz to even Michael Cole on commentary. WWE's TV-PG rating had drastically watered down the product and the promos up to that point, but those limitations didn't seem to apply to The Great One.

Rock came back as only he could and injected new life into WWE at a time when it was sorely needed.

2. The Rock Becomes a "Corporate" Champion (Survivor Series 1998)

The Deadly Games tournament WWE held for their vacant world championship remains one of the company's most compelling concepts, if only for the vast amount of stories told in that one night at Survivor Series 1998.

Save for two matches for the women's and tag team titles, the entire event was built around the crowning of a new champ. Mr. McMahon was determined to ensure the gold didn't fall back into the grasp of his archnemesis "Stone Cold" Steve Austin by backing Mankind at every turn.

The show will never be remembered for having outstanding action, but the storytelling that was weaved throughout a majority of the matches made it a must-see tourney. Rock entered the finals against Mankind as the underdog, only to cheat him out of the win and reveal that he had been in cahoots with the McMahons from the get-go.

It was a brilliant swerve (and a rare retread of the Montreal Screwjob that was actually acceptable) that gave Rock his first world title, aligned him with the top heels in the company and cemented his status as a perennial main event player.

Hulk Hogan vs. "Stone Cold" Steve Austin looked to be the biggest bout WWE could do at WrestleMania 18 upon Hogan's return to the company after almost a decade away. Instead, WWE went with The Rock facing Hogan in a match that was far better than it had any right to be on paper.

Rock was firmly established as a household name by that point, so it wasn't a case of him needing to be endorsed by Hogan. Rather, it was billed as a battle between the past and present of the industry, and if anyone could help Hogan see the light and return to his roots as a fan favorite, it was Rock.

It's the quintessential "sports entertainment" match in that it was all about the energy in the SkyDome that night and not as much about the moves themselves. The Toronto crowd ate up everything they did and rallied behind Hogan despite him being portrayed as the heel.

Hogan couldn't have asked for a better opponent than Rock in his first outing on The Grandest Stage of Them All since 1993. They quickly clicked and produced a certified spectacle.

Rock triumphed over Hogan with one of his patented People's Elbows, but Hogan was the true winner with the audience accepting him as a babyface once again. While Hogan gained more from that match than Rock did, both were responsible for making that WrestleMania moment as iconic as it was.

Graham Mirmina, aka Graham "GSM" Matthews, has specialized in sports and entertainment writing since 2010. Visit his website, WrestleRant , and subscribe to his YouTube channel for more wrestling-related content.

articles.title: Ranking the Top 9 Players to Watch in Men's College Basketball
articles.summary: Three weeks into the 2026-27 men's college basketball season, must-watch sensations are already popping up all over the country.
articles.body:
Three weeks into the 2026-27 men's college basketball season, must-watch sensations are already popping up all over the country.

To be clear from the outset, this is not intended to be a ranking of National Player of the Year candidates, nor is it anything close to a mock draft. Rather, it's a ranking of players we plan on watching as often as possible over the course of the next four months, simply because they already have been enjoyable to watch.

Now, is there a fair amount of overlap between this list of players and the various mock drafts and Wooden Award odds out there?

However, try not to lose your mind if your favorite projected lottery pick or semi-longshot for the Wooden Award didn't make the cut.

It's still early, after all, and these are merely the main attractions thus far.

Statistics current through the start of play on Sunday.

Amari Allen, Alabama —Had a triple-double (16 points, 13 rebounds, 12 assists) against Arkansas State and should continue to flourish with the Crimson Tide's breakneck pace of play.

Cruz Davis, Texas Tech —Hofstra transfer paced Red Raiders to marquee win over Illinois.

Thijs De Ridder, Virginia —Preseason ACC Player of the Year does more than a little bit of everything for a Cavaliers team that has already emerged as a serious title contender.

Silas Demary Jr., Connecticut —Huskies might have the best backcourt in the country, and this senior is the leader of it.

Donovan Dent, LSU —Any time you're hate-watching LSU, you're going to love watching Dent, who already has three points-assists double-doubles.

Mason Falslev, Utah State —Aggies head coach changes seemingly every year, but Falslev is the star who just keeps getting better.

Caleb Holt, Arizona —Arguably the most tantalizing talent in this year's draft class, Holt only didn't make the ranked list because we already have one of his teammates on it.

Dior Johnson, UCF —Walking bucket who will do everything in his power to carry UCF back to the NCAA tournament.

Nikola Kusturica, UCLA —17-year-old freshman who already does it all and is only going to get better with age.

Jordan Smith Jr., Arkansas —Young Arkansas team is still finding its footing, but Smith will eventually be a wrecking ball for John Calipari.

Andrej Stojakovic, Illinois —Super-early candidate for NPOY after decimating Duke in Durham, but teammates Quentin Coleman and (once healthy) David Mirkovic are probably even bigger must-watch players. (Illinois is scary, y'all.)

Matas Vokietaitis, Texas —Might not take a shot more than 10 feet from the hoop all season long, but this seven-footer might also be the most physically dominant player in the entire country.

Robert Wright III, BYU —He sometimes overshadowed freshman superstar AJ Dybantsa last year, and this scoring machine is going to steal the spotlight from Bruce Branch III on a regular basis this year.

2026-27 Stats : 23.3 PPG, 5.5 APG, 2.5 SPG, 41.2% 3PT, .238 WS/40

Memphis has been one of the big surprises of the first three weeks of this season, beating then-ranked Iowa State on a neutral court on opening night, clipping VCU at home a few days later and then blowing out Louisville last weekend.

There was also a 24-point loss to Vanderbilt in between the VCU and Louisville games. But the Tigers still have one of the best NCAA tournament resumes, if you're into that sort of thing in November.

Well, the singular star of those three wins was Jayden Reid.

He scored 26 points against the Cyclones, including single-handedly outscoring Iowa State 11-7 after the game was tied at 69-69.

He put up a career-high 32 points with seven assists against VCU, including the game-tying and game-winning free throws with five seconds remaining.

And his best game yet came against the Cardinals, when he filled out the stat sheet to the tune of 24 points, 10 assists, five rebounds and four steals (with just one turnover).

It's all very reminiscent of PJ Haggerty's lone season with the Tigers. When Reid is in his bag, Memphis has the offense to hang with anyone. And if this team's defense continues to be as underwhelming as it has been thus far, there could be a lot of "put the team on my back" nights from Reid.

2026-27 Stats : 22.6 PPG, 8.0 RPG, 4.8 APG, 1.8 SPG, 40.0% 3PT, .235 WS/40

Freshman Caleb Holt is the Arizona star who could wind up going No. 1 overall in next summer's draft.

But sophomore Ivan Kharchenkov is the Wildcat who has been consistently taking over games with both versatility and intensity.

He might be the first player in college basketball history to record a quadruple-double consisting of points, assists, rebounds and guttural screams to the fans in the stands.

Kharchenkov sure did open the year with a bang—albeit in a losing effort—going for 38 points and 10 rebounds against UCLA.

He proceeded to score at least 16 points in each of his next four games. He also had at least seven rebounds in three of the four and continued to make an impact as a playmaker. He led the Wildcats in scoring in their statement win over Connecticut.

On top of more than doubling his assist rate compared to last year and becoming a much more assertive presence on offense, Kharchenkov has shown a purer three-point stroke than he did a year ago. He'll surely be a lottery pick if that remains the case.

2026-27 Stats : 20.5 PPG, 5.2 APG, 2.0 SPG, 23.8% 3PT, .207 WS/40

Four of the top seven players on this list were part of last week's Players Era 8, so here's hoping you watched as much of that tournament as you possibly could.

However, it was West Virginia's freshman lead guard Miles Sadler who really used that trip to Las Vegas to catapult onto the national radar.

By all accounts, he had a sensational senior year of high school and subsequent summer, despite getting snubbed from the McDonald's All-American Game. But if you missed the memo on Sadler amid an offseason littered with lawsuits, tournament expansion and all sorts of off-the-court to-dos, he sure did announce his presence with a combined 70 points, 10 assists and eight steals against Auburn, Kansas and Florida.

It was the game against the Jayhawks that he really took over. Maybe it would have been a different story if Kansas had Melvin Council or Tyran Stokes available in that one, but Sadler capitalized to the tune of 34 points, nearly leading the Mountaineers to what would have been a substantial upset.

We shall see if the perimeter jumper develops into a more reliable asset, because it's already clear he's going to let it fly. Sadler went 5-for-25 from distance in Vegas and is taking more than 38 percent of his team's shots while on the floor. If he starts hitting them at a better clip, the "smaller Trae Young" comparisons will almost write themselves.

2026-27 Stats : 18.7 PPG, 6.2 RPG, 3.5 APG, 2.8 SPG, 20.0% 3PT, .362 WS/40

Tyler Tanner was the national breakout star of yesteryear, blossoming from a freshman reserve who mostly played because of his defense into a sophomore sensation who ranked fourth in points, third in assists and first in steals among SEC players.

But after measuring in at 5'10¾" and 166.8 pounds at the NBA draft combine, he elected to return to Vanderbilt, hit the weight room and try to prove that he can shine at the next level in spite of his height.

So far, so good. Tanner had 17 points and a game-high (and career-high) 10 rebounds in Vanderbilt's rout of Wake Forest. He also had 17 points, five rebounds and three steals in their 24-point victory over Memphis, shining in that head-to-head battle with the aforementioned Jayden Reid. And then on Friday against UCF, he reset his career high for rebounds with 11 boards to go along with 23 points and four assists.

His three-point stroke hasn't been there yet, but he made 60 triples at a 37 percent clip last year. Got to think those will eventually start to fall as he gets even more national attention than last year while attempting to steer Vanderbilt to its first Final Four and/or its first year as a top-two seed in the Dance.

2026-27 Stats : 17.6 PPG, 6.9 RPG, 2.7 APG, 51.4% 3PT, .276 WS/40

Most of the upper echelon players to watch are ball-dominant guards who seemingly need to touch the ball in order for that half-court offense to function.

Thomas Haugh, on the other hand, is more of a 6'9" Energizer Bunny who both gets better every year and seems to have been in college for a decade at this point.

In reality, this is his fourth season at Florida, and he has been Mr. Everything for the Gators amid their rigorous early schedule.

Right off the bat, he went for 19 points, 10 rebounds and four assists in the opening win over Miami. He also had 21 and 10 against Florida State before averaging 18 per game in the Players Era 8 against Notre Dame, Houston and West Virginia.

We don't have NET rankings yet for bracketology purposes, but all five of those games played away from home are likely to be Quad 1 results. Haugh shone in all of them.

And after shooting just 32.6 percent from distance as more of a volume scorer last season, he has gone 18-for-35 on three-point attempts through his first seven games.

That was (presumably) the one thing holding Haugh back from leaving for the NBA after last season. If he continues to do a solid Milan Momcilovic impersonation along the perimeter while also continuing to play with his hair on fire, he might be getting sized for a second national championship ring in a few months' time.

2026-27 Stats : 17.8 PPG, 6.8 RPG, 4.4 APG, 2.6 SPG, 37.0% 3PT, .342 WS/40

Andrej Stojakovic dominated the headlines with his 46-point performance in Illinois' 21-point road win over Duke.

However, it was freshman Quentin Coleman who stole the show, seemingly everywhere all of the time en route to 27 points, eight rebounds, four assists, three steals and one iconic wink.

His statistics are plenty noteworthy, but it's his aura on the court that will make him a must-watch player who we marvel at on a weekly basis.

Coleman was also huge for the Illini in the road game against Texas Tech, shooting 5-for-6 from three-point range and finishing with 19 points, five rebounds, four assists and two steals as they nearly pulled off an unbelievable comeback.

What's absurd about how impressive he has already been is that he hasn't even been feeling well.

The flu has been ravaging the Illinois locker room to the point where Coleman threw up during both of those marquee games. He also missed Friday's game against Eastern Illinois. Still, he is already looking like even more of a superstar than Keaton Wagler was for this team one year ago.

We can't wait to see what he can do once he's past hugging a trash can at halftime.

2026-27 Stats : 20.0 PPG, 5.7 APG, 1.7 SPG, .302 WS/40

The constant for Houston over the past decade has been tenacity. The players change, but it's just a given at this point that the Cougars are going to be proficient on the offensive glass and a real pain in the you-know-what to try to score against.

The variable has been the lead guard, with Houston elevating from "a really good team" to "probably the best team in the country" every time a Marcus Sasser, Jamal Shead or Kingston Flemings flipped a switch and started taking games over on a regular basis.

And in Dedan Thomas Jr., it is abundantly clear that the Cougars have a special talent who could lead them to the first national championship in program history.

He averaged 13.6 points and 5.1 assists per game as a freshman at UNLV in 2023-24, but watching him play with legitimate talent around him has already been a delight.

Between the consecutive wins over Florida and Kansas in the Players Era 8, Thomas racked up 46 points, 10 assists and four steals with just one turnover. He went a perfect 14-for-14 from the charity stripe, and it felt like he could get either to the rim or to the free-throw line whenever he darn well pleased.

Injuries cut short his last two seasons—a shoulder in 2024-25 and a foot in 2025-26—but Houston is already looking like this year's team to beat, provided he stays healthy.

2026-27 Stats : 16.7 PPG, 9.3 APG, 1.0 SPG, 37.5% 3PT, .343 WS/40

Jeremy Fears Jr. was already a Wooden All-America First Team player last season, and it's not often that those guys stay in college.

In fact, that 10-man "roster" consisted of Fears, six lottery picks, two other top 40 picks and JT Toppin, who almost certainly would have been a first-round pick if he hadn't torn his ACL and opted for another year in college.

In other words, Fears wasn't exactly a difficult choice for preseason All-American, and he has thus far been every bit as good as he was last year, if not better.

One big development compared to last season is how frequently Fears is marching to the free-throw line.

In an otherwise disastrous night for the Spartans in a 61-46 loss to Tennessee this past Tuesday, Fears went 16-for-18 from the charity stripe. He also attempted 17 free throws in the Champions Classic victory over Duke and is drawing a senior-year-Zach-Edey-like 9.3 fouls per 40 minutes played.

Even at that, it often feels like he isn't being selfish enough, with more assists (56) than official field-goal attempts (43) through six games.

In Fears' hands, though, this could be Tom Izzo's best team since the one that Mateen Cleaves led to a national championship in 2000.

2026-27 Stats : 16.2 PPG, 8.6 RPG, 1.8 APG, 46.7% 3PT, .225 WS/40

When you're operating at less than full strength, there is not a team in the country you would rather avoid than Houston, because of how relentlessly physical that team is.

But after missing Wednesday's game against West Virginia with a bone bruise in his knee, Tyran Stokes gave Kansas 32 minutes, 22 points and 11 rebounds in Thursday's loss to the Cougars, almost propelling them to an improbable comeback.

He's no Cooper Flagg. He's probably no AJ Dybantsa or Darryn Peterson, either. But Stokes is the early favorite to go No. 1 overall in the 2027 NBA draft and has thus far looked the part.

We already noted his line against Houston. He also had 23 points (including four triples), 10 rebounds and four assists as Kansas routed Kentucky in the Champions Classic. And before the bone bruise occurred against UNLV, he had 13 points and 10 rebounds in just 13 minutes played.

Bill Self brought back Tre White and Melvin Council and brought in Trey Kaufman-Renn and Keanu Dawes to ensure his star freshman would be surrounded by a bevy of veterans. However, it is already clear that this team goes as Stokes goes.

If that early three-point percentage is legitimate, this 6'8" bull in a china shop is going to be the third consecutive freshman to win the Wooden Award.

articles.title: Power Ranking Every NBA Team's Defense So Far
articles.summary: It's been a solid few years of NBA basketball for the old adage "defense wins championships."
articles.body:
It's been a solid few years of NBA basketball for the old adage "defense wins championships."

The 2023-24 Boston Celtics, 2024-25 Oklahoma City Thunder and 2025-26 New York Knicks ranked third , first and 10th in their respective seasons in points allowed per 100 possessions.

And several of the best teams in the league right now are dominating on that end.

So today, we're breaking down the entire league by where each team ranks defensively. But we're not just going to sort them by defensive rating. That's easy enough to do on your own.

Here, we'll certainly pay close attention to that number, but recent performance and defensive talent on every roster are also under consideration. Potential is another factor. And obviously, given those last couple pieces of criteria, subjectivity is in the mix here.

Based on all of the above, here's where every team ranks based on defense alone right now.

Numbers courtesy of NBA.com/stats, Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass and current through November 21, 2026.

This was always going to be a down year for the Milwaukee Bucks, but the post-Giannis Antetokounmpo era has gotten off to an even worse start than many expected.

And bad defense from players who should be better is a big reason why.

Defensive estimated plus-minus still has Myles Turner as a plus on that end, but he looks heavy, slow and uninterested in most possessions. Kyle Kuzma, who's had a few positive-impact years in the past, has been a non-factor on that end too.

And beyond what that's doing to this season's defense, the veterans aren't setting much of an example for the younger players. They're also potentially tanking their own trade value.

It's tough to keep a competent, consistent defense on the floor while starting a rookie point guard, especially when that's far from the roster's only problem.

The Sacramento Kings' first five includes the trio of Darius Acuff Jr., Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis, all of whom are behind their positional peers as defenders.

And even if Keegan Murray and De'Andre Hunter have their moments as multi-positional wing and forward defenders, they're nowhere near good enough to overcome the hole their highest-usage players put them in on that end.

It's hard to imagine the Brooklyn Nets being anything but one of the worst defenses in the NBA all season.

Day'Ron Sharpe may be the only rotation player you can confidently say is somewhere between good and great on that end. And lack of defensive talent might not even be the biggest problem.

Brooklyn's offense is almost entirely dependent on Julius Randle and Michael Porter Jr., both of whom have been among the league's easiest defensive targets for years.

It's hard to judge anything the Chicago Bulls have done this season, because so much seemed designed to maximize Caleb Wilson before he went down with a hand injury.

That includes the defense, which was dramatically worse when the rookie forward was on the floor. But regardless of what happens with Wilson, there isn't a ton of upside for this unit.

Nic Claxton and Jalen Smith can be solid inside, but neither is spectacular defensively. And Chicago may not have a single defender on the perimeter who's a clear plus.

The tricky thing about analyzing the Phoenix Suns is that their starters are probably worse than the second unit. And that certainly applies to the defensive end of the floor.

To a pretty stunning degree, the team allows more points per 100 possessions when any of Dillon Brooks, Jalen Green or Devin Booker is on the floor. And though that's not true of Miles Bridges, he's certainly prone to lapses on that end too.

Add to that the fact that Khaman Maluach still appears to be a long way away from competence as a defensive anchor, and it's tough to see this group getting significantly better between now and the end of the season.

The absence of Stephen Curry is obviously the Golden State Warriors' biggest problem, but it isn't their only one.

Their best defender is 36-year-old Draymond Green. Even at this age and in spite of the fact that he's actively hurt their offense since the start of 2025-26, they're relying on him to keep the defense anywhere near average.

It craters when their second-best player, rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, is on the floor. And there aren't many others on the roster who can reliably create shots.

So, the options are to rely on the younger forward and get destroyed on defense or rely on the veteran and struggle to score.

They've done a decent job of finding something of a balance there, but even that has led to a below-average defense overall.

The Charlotte Hornets have multiple good defenders, including Sion James (stout and switchable on the perimeter), Moussa Diabaté (a solid rim protector who also takes possessions away from opponents as an offensive rebounder) and Naz Reid (who moves well for a player his size).

But no one on the roster stands out as a spectacular defensive anchor or point-of-attack bulldog. And the talent hasn't really coalesced yet.

This is a team that can certainly get better on the defensive end, though. Players like James, Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel all have the potential to improve over the coming weeks and months.

It took Jamahl Mosley a little too long to come to the realization that he needed to start Herbert Jones and play him heavy minutes to be competitive.

But we're there now, and as long as the New Orleans Pelicans' best and most tenacious defender remains a fixture in the rotation, this group has a lot of room to move up.

When Jones is on the floor, New Orleans allows 108.1 points per 100 possessions, a defensive rating that ranks in the 88th percentile. When he's off the floor, that number explodes to an almost unimaginable 133.4.

If the Pelicans would simply build more lineups around him, Yves Missi and Trey Murphy III, they'd at least be passable on this end.

The Washington Wizards' defense should be better, at least on paper.

Anthony Davis, Alex Sarr and AJ Dybantsa give them a huge, versatile frontcourt. Kyshawn George, Bilal Coulibaly and Dybantsa, in theory, should provide plenty of switchability along with their length.

But defensive units are often only as strong as their weakest link. And when Trae Young is on the floor, Washington has a 44th percentile defensive rating. It tanks all the way down to the 27th percentile when Young plays without AD.

With at least one easy target for opposing offenses to pick on and Dybantsa and George still figuring out how to make a positive defensive impact, Washington may have a hard time elevating above the middle of the pack.

Despite the NBA sanctions that will affect the Los Angeles Clippers' team-building prospects for years, it felt reasonable to expect this year's team to remain competitive on defense.

Derrick Jones Jr., Kris Dunn and Brook Lopez have all had good reputations on that end for years. And Ty Lue is still one of the best coaches in the league.

But Darius Garland and rookie Keaton Wagler have both been prone to lapses. And Rui Hachimura, another player who at least has the reputation for solid defense, just hasn't made enough of an impact on that end.

This is a team that should absolutely be better on defense.

Evan Mobley is a recent Defensive Player of the Year winner, Jarrett Allen is a good defensive anchor and Peyton Watson can be a weakside, shot-blocking menace.

But Mobley and Allen have both missed a little time. Watson's defensive impact hasn't leaped off the screen quite like it did in Denver. And ultimately, there may not be a defensive frontcourt in the league that can make up for Cleveland's backcourt.

Donovan Mitchell is undersized and expending much of his energy reserves on the offensive end. And James Harden, who was never close to a high-impact defender, even in his prime, is now 37 and slowing down.

As long as opponents are able to break the perimeter as often as they do against these two, it's going to be tough for the Cavs to win at the rate they have in previous years.

The Utah Jazz certainly have some defensive talent on both the interior and perimeter, but injuries to Jaren Jackson Jr. and Jusuf Nurkić have severely weakened the interior, while inexperience has hurt the perimeter defense.

So, even though the Jazz are in the bottom half of the league in points allowed per 100 possessions, there's a lot of upward potential here.

As Ace Bailey and Darryn Peterson get more used to defending NBA offenses and JJJ and Nurkić trickle back into the rotation, this defense should get a lot better.

You knew it would only be a matter of time before the Giannis Antetokounmpo version of the Miami Heat started stringing together wins, but their surge has a lot more to do with the offense than the defense.

That's a little surprising, considering coach Erik Spoelstra's pedigree and individual talents like Bam Adebayo, Davion Mitchell and Giannis Antetokounmpo. But opponents have had a lot of success attacking weaker links like Klay Thompson and Andrew Wiggins.

Given the size, talent level and coaching this organization has, expect them to figure some things out over the next few weeks.

Even without Dereck Lively II, the Dallas Mavericks have a ton of interesting young defensive talent in Cooper Flagg, Morez Johnson Jr. and Zaccharie Risacher.

All of the above just need a little more time to learn the nuances of NBA defense and how to operate as a cohesive unit.

In the meantime, Daniel Gafford is a good anchor who'll cover up a lot of their mistakes as they learn.

For years, the Orlando Magic winning games has largely depended on intensity, physicality and consistent defensive effort.

Without that, their often uninspiring offense just can't carry them far enough. That's generally been the case this season with Orlando hovering around the middle of the league defensively.

But two of Orlando's more versatile defenders, Paolo Banchero and Jalen Suggs, have missed a lot of time this season. And while it's hard to bet on durability with this roster, if those two can stay on the court for an extended stretch, this team will climb.

The Toronto Raptors having a ho-hum defense, even without Kawhi Leonard, is a little concerning.

Scottie Barnes, Collin Murray-Boyles, Jamal Shead and Jakob Poeltl are all, at least historically, plus defenders. Even RJ Barrett has had his moments as a switchable forward/wing.

But right now, the unit isn't jelling. It's allowing too many shots at the rim. And when Poeltl is off the floor, that's spelled trouble.

Assuming Leonard comes back soon, this is a group that should almost certainly improve, though.

Entering this season, the consensus opinion on the Los Angeles Lakers was that they'd dominate on offense and be dominated on defense. Ideally, Luka Dončić would be able to do just enough on the one end to make up for the other.

And while one part of that opinion has proven true (L.A. is fourth on offense and Luka is putting up historic numbers), it looks like the other may have just been wrong.

The Lakers aren't going to become one of the best defenses in the league, but they're firmly above average, and a pair of offseason additions are big reasons why.

Walker Kessler is the obvious one. His rim protection, 2.1 blocks per game and 7.1 defensive rebounds in 30.9 minutes make him one of the best anchors in the league. Matisse Thybulle is the less obvious game-changer. His attention on the ball and playmaking off of it make him one of the best perimeter defenders in the league.

And when both Kessler and Thybulle are on the floor, L.A. is giving up just 108.9 points per 100 possessions (a mark that ranks in the 84th percentile).

The Indiana Pacers miss Tyrese Haliburton, but his absence obviously affects the offense far more than it does the other end. In fact, some of their plus defenders are why this team is able to survive Haliburton's latest injury.

Ivica Zubac is still a high-end defensive rebounder and is good at simply being in the right spots and taking up a ton of space. And from there, Indiana has multiple good (though maybe not great) switchable defenders around Zubac in Aaron Nesmith, Pascal Siakam and Andrew Nembhard.

And once Haliburton comes back, the pressure that his offense puts on opponents will sap them of energy and make them a little easier to defend on the other end.

For the first time in his career, Joel Embiid has been objectively bad (or at least below average) on the offensive end.

Lack of explosiveness is just part of the game for him now, and that's meant more jump shooting. More jump shooting means more long rebounds (and transition opportunities for the opposition), and he still turns the ball over at a pretty high rate too.

So you might think that playing this slower version of Embiid along with the undersized Tyrese Maxey and soon-to-be-42-year-old LeBron James would give the Philadelphia 76ers some major defensive problems, but his sheer size and shot-blocking instincts are keeping this team afloat on that end.

The Sixers are solidly above average and allowing 8.1 fewer points per 100 possessions when Embiid is on the floor. And combining his anchoring ability with VJ Edgecombe's tenacity outside gives Philly a shot at a top-10 defense.

It still doesn't quite feel like the Denver Nuggets have clawed their way back to Tier 1 contender status, but they've looked a bit more like that lately. And surprisingly, it's their defensive effort that's turning them around.

Perhaps even more surprising still, their traditionally offense-first superstars, Jamal Murray and Nikola Jokić, are leading the charge on that end.

Defensive box plus/minus openly acknowledges its own shortcomings in measuring defense, but Murray is posting an above- average mark there for the first time in his career. And Jokić is leading the team with a plus-1.2 defensive estimated plus-minus (one of the more trusted catch-alls in NBA front offices).

When they're together, Denver allows 110.2 points per 100 possessions, a defensive rating that ranks in the 80th percentile.

The Houston Rockets are winning more with their offense than they are on the other end, but they boast a combination of defensive talent and experience that should help them climb this leaderboard.

Amen Thompson hasn't been quite as consistent as his twin brother on that end, but he's still good for multiple jaw-dropping defensive highlights per game. And fellow youngsters Jabari Smith Jr. and Tari Eason also move the needle in the right direction with their size and switchability.

Add some veteran tricks from the likes of Marcus Smart and Steven Adams to the mix, and it's easy to imagine this becoming a championship-caliber resistance.

Much has been made of Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart's offensive struggles. That contributing to a middle-of-the-road offensive rating is a little concerning, but the foundation of a good title defense is still in place.

Those two and OG Anunoby give New York one of the most tenacious and versatile trios of wing defenders in the league. And Karl-Anthony Towns, after spending much of his career fielding criticism over his defense, leads the NBA in both rebounds and defensive rebounds per game.

With those four and Andre Drummond and Jose Alvarado coming off the bench, the Knicks have more than enough defense to make up for any shortcomings the undersized Jalen Brunson might have on that end.

The Oklahoma City Thunder's defense doesn't have the same ceiling without Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace and Chet Holmgren.

The team's 2-4 in its last six, and it's allowing 115.7 points per game during that stretch.

But there's still enough culture and institutional knowledge for this defense to at least be above average (its 113.7 defensive rating without those three ranks in the 58th percentile).

And it still has multiple high-end defenders in Alex Caruso, Isaiah Hartenstein, Ajay Mitchell and Kenrich Williams to survive until Chet's return.

The Portland Trail Blazers, despite starting a 36-year-old, post-Achilles tear Damian Lillard, have been one of the league's better defenses because of their depth of defensive talent around him (and a couple of legitimate defensive stars).

Toumani Camara certainly deserves a shout. He can guard all over opposing lineups and brings a rarely matched tenacity to every matchup. Jrue Holiday is one of the headiest defenders in the NBA. And Donovan Clingan is simply massive, is almost always in the right spot and has been phenomenal at cleaning up the few lapses this defense has made.

Even their top offensive players, Lillard and Deni Avdija, are at least competing on that end. And this group figures to be, at the very least, in the top half of the league all season.

Zach Edey may be the only truly game-changing defender on the Memphis Grizzlies. And despite aggressive management of his workload, he's unquestionably the biggest reason this team ranks as high as it does defensively.

Edey only plays 20.8 minutes per game, but when he's on the floor, the Grizzlies allow just 99.5 points per 100 possessions.

They are, unsurprisingly, dominating Edey's stretches to a degree that near-average play without him is more than enough to win games. And with Cedric Coward, Jaylen Wells and Cameron Boozer, they're getting more than enough near-average defense in those non-Edey minutes.

The Atlanta Hawks have a couple rotation staples in Jalen Johnson and CJ McCollum who are tabbed as below-average defenders by defensive estimated plus-minus .

But after that, this team is loaded with defensive length, athleticism and tenacity.

The tip of the spear is Dyson Daniels, who leads the league in steals per game at 2.9 and is a solid positional rebounder. Surrounding him with Nickeil Alexander-Walker and Onyeka Okongwu makes this a turnover-generating machine that forces giveaways on 17.8 percent of opponents' possessions (the second -best mark in the league).

Jalen Duren isn't a Rudy Gobert-level rim protector or anything, but he's a key cog in one of the league's best defenses. So, the fact that the Detroit Pistons rank fifth in points allowed per 100 possessions despite playing most of this season without him is a testament to some of the best perimeter defenders in the league.

Ron Holland is a high-end athlete who seems to take every matchup he's given personally. Javonte Green is providing steals and veteran know-how to around the same degree he did last season. Even their offensive engine, Cade Cunningham, is a better defender than most creators tasked with his level of responsibility on the other end.

But the biggest driver of Detroit's success on defense is undoubtedly Ausar Thompson. He can throw just about any guard or wing off their usual level of production. He's an absolute menace in passing lanes and around loose dribbles. And even as a 6'7" wing, he leads Detroit in defensive rebounds per game.

The Boston Celtics are even better defensively than they were last season for a few reasons.

First, the combination of Jayson Tatum and Paul George is undoubtedly better than Jaylen Brown and the empty roster spot dedicated to Tatum till he returned from injury last season. Even after an Achilles tear for Tatum and at age 36 for George, both are still capable of guarding multiple positions and bothering most matchups.

Another factor is the continued emergence of Neemias Queta, whose shot-blocking is a great backdrop for the star duo.

And with several others—including Derrick White, Baylor Scheierman and Hugo González—providing above-average to great defensive contributions, it's safe to assume Boston will have one of the best defenses in the league throughout the season.

If it weren't for the alien who won the first unanimous Defensive Player of the Year in NBA history last season, Rudy Gobert would be on track to win the award for a fifth time.

One of the greatest defensive anchors and rim protectors of all time, even at 34, is still dominating on that end. When he's on the floor, the Minnesota Timberwolves give up just 98.3 points per 100 possessions, and their opponents shoot 58.7 percent at the rim (a mark that ranks in the 91st percentile).

But Gobert is far from the only reason the Timberwolves have the top defensive rating in the NBA.

Jaden McDaniels' and Jonathan Kuminga's size and switchability have been huge. Ayo Dosunmu, though he's obviously a worse all-around player than Anthony Edwards, is probably better for defensive consistency. And even LaMelo Ball looks as locked in on that end as he's ever been.

We've never seen a player produce like Victor Wembanyama.

Right now, he's averaging 11.7 defensive rebounds, 4.8 blocks and 1.6 steals per 75 possessions. And forget the steals: No one in league history has matched or exceeded both of those averages for defensive rebounds and blocks for an entire season.

With Wemby on the backline, just about any collection of NBA players could piece together a solid defense, but that's not what the San Antonio Spurs have put around their superstar.

Stephon Castle, Dylan Harper and Devin Vassell have all been clear defensive pluses. Even the smallest member of that starting five, De'Aaron Fox, is contributing with a high steal rate and a very strong defensive rebounding rate for a point guard.

There are certainly concerns when some of those starters head to the bench, but there's more than enough evidence here to support San Antonio taking this top spot.

articles.title: Pontefract Paralympian Lee Fryer charged with 11 counts of rape
articles.summary: Paris 2024 silver medalist Lee Fryer will stand trial in March charged with 11 counts of rape.
articles.body:
An athlete who won a silver medal for Britain at the 2024 Paralympics in Paris has been charged with 11 counts of rape.

Wheelchair basketball player Lee Fryer, 26, from Pontefract, West Yorkshire, faces 17 charges in total, including voyeurism, intentional strangulation, assault and possession of a class A drug, namely cocaine.

He appeared at Leeds Crown Court on Thursday, where he pleaded not guilty to all the charges except voyeurism, for which no plea was entered. He is due to stand trial on 22 March next year.

British Wheelchair Basketball (BWB) confirmed he had been removed from the GB programme and all British Wheelchair Basketball activities when he was arrested in July.

Fryer is also charged with controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate relationship and perverting the course of justice.

A BWB spokeperson said: "We are aware of the criminal charges brought against Lee Fryer and recognise the seriousness of the allegations.

"At the point of his arrest, he was removed from the GB Programme and all British Wheelchair Basketball activities, pending the outcome of the external investigation.

"As criminal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this time."

ParalympicsGB said: "We are aware there are charges against Lee Fryer.

"As the matter is now subject to ongoing legal proceedings we will not be commenting further at this stage."

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds , catch up with the latest episode of Look North .

images.caption: Lee Fryer is due to face trial at Leeds Crown Court next March

articles.title: New Lakers Rumors Reveal Luka Doncic, JJ Redick's Impact on Quentin Grimes' Contract
articles.summary: Quentin Grimes had two powerful voices advocating for his signing before he joined the Los Angeles Lakers, according to The Stein Line's Marc Stein.
articles.body:
Quentin Grimes had two powerful voices advocating for his signing before he joined the Los Angeles Lakers, according to The Stein Line's Marc Stein .

Stein reported that Grimes "received a very strong endorsement" from Lakers star Luka Dončić, who he was briefly teammates with on the Dallas Mavericks. Coach JJ Redick was in favor of the move as well.

"There was confidence within the organization that Grimes could not only bring a trusted catch-and-shoot prowess to Lakerland but also play more consistently closer to the level that resulted in the 6-foot-4 guard averaging 21.9 points per game for Philadelphia across the final 28 games of the 2024-25 season," per Stein.

Grimes has been exactly what Los Angeles hoped. Through 15 games, he's averaging 12.7 points and shooting 41.2 percent from beyond the arc.

The 26-year-old has also stepped up after moving into the starting lineup with Austin Reaves battling a heel injury. His 47 points in the 118-114 overtime win against the Charlotte Hornets were a career high.

Since his arrival in the Lakers' front office, Rob Pelinka has succeeded in bringing big stars to Southern California, be it Dončić, LeBron James, Anthony Davis or Russell Westbrook. The team continually hit a wall, however, because Pelinka and others didn't identify the right supporting pieces around those star players.

Grimes is the kind of signing the Lakers weren't landing with enough regularity.

Maybe his hot start is a mirage and he'll regress in the coming months. He has never shot better than 38.6 percent on three-pointers over a full season. With the way he's playing right now, his four-year, $60 million contract looks like a home run.

For his part, Dončić seemed to have a keen understanding of how much he and Grimes would complement one another on the court.

Los Angeles Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka doesn't plan to sit idly by with the team off to a 14-3 start.

Pelinka said last week on Spectrum SportsNet the team will "be active at the trade deadline to shore up things that we see." He emphasized the front office wants to be aggressive because the team is performing so well (8:45 mark):

The Stein Line's Marc Stein reported Sunday that center is one specific area of focus. The Lakers are "actively searching" for options at the position.

Walker Kessler has appeared in 16 games and averaged 14.3 points, 10.7 rebounds and 2.1 blocks. Backup center Sandro Mamukelashvili is providing solid depth off the bench as well.

Still, there's a noticeable drop defensively at the position whenever Kessler isn't on the floor, and Los Angeles doesn't want to pin all of its hopes to a player who has missed significant time in the past through injuries.

The Lakers are also seriously lacking in size when you remove Kessler from the mix. He's the only regular in the rotation who's taller than 6'9".

Fortifying the center situation will be easier said than done, though.

Pelinka sacrificed a lot of draft capital in the Kessler trade, and the team doesn't have many attractive reserves it can afford to part with. In the case of Jarred Vanderbilt, his $12.4 million salary is helpful from a financial perspective, but his value around the league is probably low given how he's playing.

Pelinka pulled a rabbit out of his hat and reshuffled the roster on the fly ahead of the 2023 trade deadline. Maybe he can work his magic again and land a meaningful piece despite having limited resources.

articles.standfirst: El base de los Lakers tiene un 40,29% de tasa de uso (porcentaje de posesiones que un jugador finaliza mientras está en pista con un tiro de campo, tiro libre o pérdida) y nadie ganó el anillo con más de un 35%
articles.summary: El base de los Lakers tiene un 40,29% de tasa de uso (porcentaje de posesiones que un jugador finaliza mientras está en pista con un tiro de campo, tiro libre o pérdida) y nadie ganó el anillo con más de un 35%
articles.body: El inicio de temporada de Luka Doncic ha sido histórico. Se mantiene como máximo anotador de la NBA con 37,2 puntos de media, acumula siete partidos de 40 y dos de 50, sus registros anotadores le han colocado sólo por detrás de Michael Jordan y Wilt Chamberlain y es el único jugador de la historia que ha alcanzado los 550 puntos, los 100 rebotes y las 100 asistencias en los primeros 15 encuentros de una campaña. Sin embargo, hay un pero. Uno que, atendiendo a la estadística histórica, le impedirá ganar el anillo. El base de los Lakers tiene un 40,29% de tasa de uso, porcentaje de posesiones del equipo que un solo jugador finaliza mientras está en la cancha mediante un tiro de campo, un tiro libre o una pérdida de balón. Y aquí viene el dato negativo: ningún jugador en la historia de la NBA ha sido campeón con un porcentaje superior al 35%. En la estadística de esta temporada, Doncic es líder destacado. A su habitual peso ofensivo en el equipo se ha sumado en los últimos encuentros la ausencia de Austin Reaves, segunda referencia de los Lakers, con lo que el base esloveno ha tenido que asumir aún más responsabilidad pese a no estar tan lucido como en el inicio del curso, quizás precisamente por ello. Detrás de él están Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (36,9%), Victor Wembanyama (35,9%) y el novato Darius Acuff Jr., que tiene barra libre en los Kings (32,9%). El registro de Doncic es el tercero más alto de la historia una temporada sólo por detrás de los de Russell Westbrook, que llegó a 41,7% en el curso 2016-17 con los Thunder, y James Harden, que alcanzó el 40,5% en el ejercicio 2018-19 con los Rockets. Ninguno de ellos ganó el título. De hecho, ambos cayeron en la segunda ronda de playoffs. A lo largo de la historia ha habido 41 jugadores que han acabado una temporada con una tasa de uso superior al 35%. Y, como menciona el periodista Ben Golliver en un artículo de ESPN, ninguno se hizo con el anillo. Ni siquiera jugadores que sí fueron campeones como Kobe Bryant o Michael Jordan. Este último llegó a estar por encima del 38% en dos de sus primeras temporadas con los Bulls, pero en sus seis títulos, ya con Scottie Pippen al lado, se movió entre el 31,7% y el 34,7%. Es una muestra más de que un solo jugador, aunque sea extraordinario y tenga estadísticas asombrosas, necesita ayuda para ganar. Shai, en 2025, fue el campeón con mayor tasa de uso en la historia, con un 34,8%. En ese equipo había siete jugadores que en Liga regular llegaron a los 10 puntos de media, incluidos Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, Aaron Wiggins... En los actuales Lakers, Doncic necesitará ayuda de Reaves, Walker Kessler, Quentin Grimes... Porque nadie puede ganar solo.

articles.title: Draymond Green Addresses Eddie Johnson in New Video, 'It's Always the Losers' Debating
articles.summary: The war of words between Golden State Warriors star Draymond Green and player-turned-broadcaster Eddie Johnson is showing no signs of slowing down.
articles.body:
The war of words between Golden State Warriors star Draymond Green and player-turned-broadcaster Eddie Johnson is showing no signs of slowing down.

Following Golden State's 88-87 win over the Boston Celtics on Sunday, Green referenced Johnson and suggested that "it's always the losers" who are the loudest in debates:

How Anthony Davis Could Land in Golden State 🛬

Johnson initially drew Green's ire when he questioned whether the four-time All-Star has a Hall of Fame-worthy resume. Green went on to claim Johnson is attempting to gain attention more than anything else:

It's not as though Johnson was the first person to push back on the idea that Green should be immortalized in the Hall of Fame. The topic goes back nearly a decade , when the Warriors were at the height of their dynastic run.

The raw numbers don't flatter Green. He's averaging 8.6 points, 6.8 rebounds, 5.6 assists and 1.3 steals for his career. The veteran forward has never been a leading on-ball figure for Golden State, either.

Green's supporters will point to his Defensive Player of the Year nod in 2016-17 on top of his nine All-Defensive honors. Focusing on his scoring totals also ignores how his playing style has made him a great offensive complement to stars Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant and Klay Thompson.

The Warriors' dynasty may not happen without Green.

When Dennis Rodman and Ben Wallace have punched their ticket to the Hall of Fame, it's difficult to picture Green not getting there. More than that, he has enjoyed the kind of career a lot of players envy.

Still, this is a conversation that continues to touch a nerve.

articles.title: Knicks superfan Timothée Chalamet returns to MSG for 1st time since NBA Finals after Lakers betrayal
articles.summary: After going viral for attending a Los Angeles Lakers game with Kylie Jenner last week, New York Knicks superfan Timothée Chalamet returned to Madison Square...
articles.body:
After going viral for attending a Los Angeles Lakers game with Kylie Jenner last week, New York Knicks superfan Timothée Chalamet returned to Madison Square Garden for his first game since the NBA Finals.

The Oscar-nominated actor was sitting courtside for the team's win over the Pacers. He was wearing a pink puffer jacket and a Knicks championship hat.

This was his first Knicks game of the season. He attended several games during the team's championship run over the summer, but he hadn't been back at the Garden since June.

He was a big part of the team's postseason run. Chalamet even traveled to away playoff games to support his team. His efforts were rewarded as he celebrated with the team and was even given a place on a float in the championship parade.

Timothée Chalamet was at the Knicks' win over the Pacers

Chalamet picked a good game to go to on Sunday, Nov. 22. They have won five games in a row after losing back-to-back to the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Indiana Pacers.

The Knicks beat the Tyrese Haliburton-less Pacers on Nov. 23 by seven points. Pascal Siakam led the team with 25 points, while Andrew Nembhard and Kelly Oubre Jr. scored 16 and 15 points, respectively.

After missing the Knicks' game against the Portland Trail Blazers, Karl-Anthony Towns returned and continued his streak of double-doubles, logging an efficient 30 points and 13 rebounds.

Josh Hart had a triple-double, scoring 10 points and logging 11 rebounds and 10 assists. Landry Shamet started in place of OG Anunoby, scoring 17 points, while Jalen Brunson scored 22 points and logged seven assists.

The Knicks are on a roll and finding their footing. They are 11-6 and in second place in the Atlantic Division. They are in the middle of a five-game home stretch, which includes a Black Friday matchup with the Miami Heat on Nov. 27.

articles.title: Where Florida ranks in Basketball Power Index after third week of play
articles.summary: The Florida Gators dropped a spot in ESPN's Basketball Power Index rankings after a 2-1 week, but remain among the top three.
articles.body:
The Florida Gators suffered their first loss of the season last Wednesday against Houston in the Players Era 8 semifinals, but still managed to win two of their three games during the tournament, prevailing over Notre Dame and West Virginia.

Now 6-1 this season after three weeks of play, Todd Golden's team finds themselves ranked third in ESPN's Basketball Power Index with a 21.5 rating — down one spot and 0.7 points from last week . That puts them 2.4 points behind top-ranked Illinois and 0.7 points behind second-ranked Duke.

Florida now has an offensive rating of 12.5 (up one full point), second only to the Illinois Illini's 14.1, and a defensive rating of 8.9 (down 1.9 points), which ranks 16th in the country. The Gators have a projected overall record of 26.3-5.7 (up 0.7 wins) and a conference tally of 13.9-4.1 (down 0.5 wins) with a 63.1% chance of winning an SEC title (down 9.8%) and the 42nd-toughest remaining strength of schedule (down from 21st-hardest).

"The College Basketball Power Index (BPI) is a measure of team strength that is meant to be the best predictor of performance going forward," ESPN explains. "BPI represents how many points above or below average a team is. Strength of Record (SOR) is a measure of team accomplishment based on how difficult a team's W-L record is to achieve. Game predictions account for opponent strength, pace of play, site, travel distance, day's rest and altitude, and are used to simulate the season 10,000 times to produce season projections."

The Orange and Blue also sits at No. 3 in the Pomeroy College Basketball Rankings with a plus-32.61 behind top-ranked Houston (+35.42) and No. 2 Illinois (+33.53). Florida is expected to fall out of the top spot of both the USA TODAY Sports Coaches Poll and AP Top 25 after Week 3 of the 2026-27 campaign.

Next up, Golden's gang returns home to host the Milwaukee Panthers inside the O'Connell Center on Tuesday night for this week's lone matchup. Tipoff is set for 7 p.m. ET and the game will be broadcast on the SEC Network+.

articles.summary: ACB surprise checks at Hyderabad’s NIMS flag tender, billing and OT lapses, unauthorised implant storage, delayed Aarogyasri bills and abnormal glove use.
articles.body: Hyderabad: The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) has found a series of irregularities at Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) after two rounds of surprise checks.ACB sleuths, along with teams from TGSAFE, the drug control department, and labour department officials conducted surprise checks at NIMS on Oct 29 and Nov 2.In the five operation theatres verified, vendors were found storing implants and consignment items worth about Rs5 crore in almirahs near the OTs and in sub-stores, without authorisation. "Doctors and nursing staff allowed it and took implants directly from vendors without raising an indent. Utility certificates were raised after use and sent to the main store with vendor invoices for billing," the ACB stated, while also adding that such a practice leaves scope for collusion, including billing for implants never used.According to ACB, in some instances, billing entries totalling Rs66 lakh were processed after patients' discharge in July, Aug and Sept, particularly under the Aarogyasri scheme, where some bills were cleared up to three months after a patient's death. The ACB also flagged abnormally high use of surgical items, citing records showing 800 pairs of gloves used for one patient in a week.Sale records missingThe main canteen was found unhygienic, with food items beyond expiry date and no FSSAI registration. articles.title: Draymond Green torches Eddie Johnson after helping Warriors snap 5-game skid
articles.summary: SAN FRANCISCO – Draymond Green has nothing left to prove to cement his future Hall of Fame case. Full stop. Green is the greatest defensive player of his gen...
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO – Draymond Green has nothing left to prove to cement his future Hall of Fame case. Full stop. Green is the greatest defensive player of his generation. He is the unsung playmaking maestro of Steve Kerr's "beautiful game" offense. He is the enforcer of the dynasty Stephen Curry built in the Bay and the catalyst of the "small-ball" basketball movement that persists to this day.

Love him or hate him, Green's resume is stamped, sealed, and gold-plated.

So it's only right that Green, amidst discourse regarding the decline in his game in his 15th season in the NBA and a heated social media feud with former NBA player and current Phoenix Suns broadcaster Eddie Johnson, provided everyone with a reminder of who he is, what he's done, and why he's synonymous with winning, locking up Jayson Tatum in isolation with the game on the line to help the Warriors eke out an 88-87 victory over the Boston Celtics to end their five-game losing streak.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"That was an incredible stop at the end on Jayson Tatum. At his core, Draymond is just an unbelievable competitor and winner," Kerr said postgame, in awe at what Green's still able to do, as the Dubs coach took an extra-long hug with his longtime player after the buzzer sounded to tell him what he means to him.

"I just told him he's a champion, and that's who he is."

"I don't know if Draymond would want me to share this, but I'll do it anyway because he shares everything with me," Kerr said with a smirk. "But he told me on the trip– we talked– and he said, 'I'll do whatever you need. If you want me to come off the bench, I'll come off the bench.'

"We're constantly collaborating together. I told him I had no desire to bring him off the bench because we got to dig this thing out with defense, and he remains one of the great defenders in the league. He showed that tonight."

Draymond Green sounds off on Eddie Johnson

And it wouldn't be a signature Draymond Green game if he didn't spit some heat after the fact.

With his back-and-forth with Johnson escalating on Twitter, which began with him questioning why Green is a future Hall of Famer with his specific statistical resume when players with better statistics didn't, Green addressed the discourse around his career and his offense that Johnson drummed up.

"As someone who can do a multitude of things on the basketball court, I would never reduce myself down to, 'You gotta go score,'" Green said. "I think, when people say that — you got guys comparing their young selves to my old selves, which is fun. Says a lot. You got people flexing their resumes. And if I flex my resume back, I'm a bully."

"And so, in this world we live in, this soft world we live in, it's like, 'Oh, he's picking on someone.' No. People are going to say what they want to say," he added. "If I have time, I respond. I usually respond once, and then just kinda let them talk to their microphone or their laptop, or in Eddie's case, whoever he has typing for him, because we know he don't know how to do those things."

Green, with a wry smile creeping up his face, didn't stop there. Working the room from the podium, as reporters and media members stifled their laughter at his sheer directness, Green continued lobbing grenades in Johnson's direction.

"I'm always gonna do what's needed, you know. I've always been that guy who does what's needed, and that'll never change," Green continued. "And if you know people want to debate what they think I should do, you notice it's never really the greats debating, and it's never the winners debating. It's always the losers and the guys who just didn't quite do it, and so let them debate. It's good for… what is it? 'Edification?'"

A reporter nodded their head. Green's grin grew even larger.

"Yeah, 'Edification.' Check it out! Download it where you get your podcasts today!"

But Johnson's back-and-forth with Green on Twitter was hardly the catalyst for his much-needed bounce-back performance in a practically must-win game against the Celtics, even if players were tossing around Johnson's name in the locker room after the game.

Over the weekend, reeling off a 0-5 road trip in which the Warriors looked hapless without Curry, Kerr, assistant coach and defensive coordinator Frank Vogel, and the rest of the coaching staff took the team to task in the film room. No one was spared. Each player, top to bottom, was shown a reel of all their defensive miscues, with a specific focus on their defeated body language.

According to rookie Yaxel Lendeborg , the discussion in the session took on a "higher tone" than what is usual, just short of screaming, as they went and diced up their lack of effort and fight at times. In a game in which they held Boston to just 87 points on 32-of-83 shooting (38.6%), it was clear the message sent was well received.

"I think it lit a fire," Green said of the film session. "It was embarrassing just looking at our effort the last few games. Yeah, you go in the five games on the street, but the message was Steph's out, great. That's no reason for our defense to suck. We heard the message, and guys stepped up to the challenge and came out with a better effort tonight. It was good for us."

The Warriors will need that kind of effort moving forward. Kerr's been consistent that the offense without Curry is what it is — bumpy, awkward, and reliant on variance. What they can control, in a very Valkyries, Natalie Nakase-esque way of thinking, is their defense. Hence why Green remains so important to these Warriors, even in the twilight of his career.

They're about to get some reinforcements, with backup point guard Brandon Williams expected to return to the fold on Wednesday. Regardless, Green will remain unapologetically assured in who he is and what he's done.

"My career speaks for itself. Their careers speak for themselves. Theirs is quiet now. Mine's still speaking," Green said of former players like Johnson questioning his resume. "I actually get a good laugh out of it. And every now and then, maybe it gives me a segment to talk about."

articles.body:
Some of the NBA's most storied franchises are going to have a new on-court look in the coming weeks.

On Monday, the Los Angeles Lakers, New York Knicks, Boston Celtics, Golden State Warriors, Detroit Pistons, Sacramento Kings and Atlanta Hawks all revealed when they will wear their "Specter" edition jerseys this season:

The bold jerseys are darker in color and were reserved for a handful of franchises.

In September, Nike and the NBA revealed the Lakers, Celtics, Philadelphia 76ers, Warriors, Pistons, Hawks and Kings were selected for the specter jerseys.

The unveiling even included a Luka Dončić Lakers version making an appearance on the runway:

The NBA's announcement explained the uniforms were "created for the teams who trace their roots back to the earliest chapters of the league" with designs that were "inspired by the franchises' history, city heritage and fan culture."

Knicks and Pistons fans in particular won't have to wait long to see the jerseys in action, as their teams will don the new looks on Sunday. New York is hosting the Hawks, while the Pistons are hosting the Orlando Magic.

As for the Lakers, they will wear their jerseys for the first time on Dec. 14 against the New Orleans Pelicans.
